name: Arooj Aftab
label: Verve
lede: A Lahore teenager whose acoustic covers spread by file-sharing became the first Pakistani Grammy winner, then made a record about the night and got Elvis Costello to play Wurlitzer on it.

eras.title: Lahore on dial-up, Berklee on scholarship
eras.text: Born in Riyadh to Pakistani parents, raised in Lahore from age 10 or 11, Aftab taught herself guitar and learned to sing by copying records. She reached Boston at 19, studied production and engineering, and was in New York by 2010 editing, scoring and gigging.

q: I make the music that I want to hear that I can't find anywhere.
years.h: Berklee: from online scholarship to the Boston campus
years.p: Aftab started with five Berklee Online courses on a scholarship, then moved to the U.S. at 19 to study music production and engineering in person.
years.xp:
According to Berklee, she took five Berklee Online courses before enrolling on campus. She has said the school gave her the vocabulary to talk to herself and to the wider world of music, and she graduated in 2010.

Wikipedia describes her as self-taught on guitar and in her singing style, so the engineering degree is the one formal training she has that shows up on every record she makes.

years.src: Stereogum: Arooj Aftab Interview · Crack Magazine · Wikipedia: Arooj Aftab
years.h: An acoustic "Hallelujah" goes around Lahore by file-sharing
years.p: Aftab's guitar-and-voice take on Leonard Cohen's song spread on file-sharing sites and email in her parents' hometown, well before Pakistan had an indie scene to put it in.
years.xp: Stereogum dates the cover to 2007; Crack describes it circulating through email and file-sharing. Wikipedia credits this cover and a version of "Mera Pyaar" with helping launch Pakistan's indie scene, and calls her one of the first musicians in the country to use the internet to promote her work.

years.h: Two weeks of classical lessons with Sara Zaman in Lahore
years.p: Crack reports Aftab's formal raga-style training was two weeks with the teacher Sara Zaman, which she built on alone.

years.src: Wikipedia: Arooj Aftab · Stereogum: Arooj Aftab Interview
years.h: Berklee degree in hand, Aftab moves to New York
years.p: She edits, scores films and sings around the jazz and new-music scene, and works audio jobs at outlets including the Huffington Post and Vice, per Stereogum.

years.h: NPR and WQXR name her one of 100 Composers Under 40
years.p: Her first national notice comes as a composer, three years before her debut album.

eras.title: A bird, then some islands
eras.text: Two records made mostly alone and mostly quiet: one acoustic, one ambient and electronic. Critics noticed, New York's new-music world took her in, and she kept a day job in film editing.

years.h: Bird Under Water: the self-released debut
years.p: Acoustic, in Urdu and English, with her voice out front. The Financial Times gave it four stars of five in March 2015.
years.xp:
Wikipedia lists the release as 2014 and independent; Berklee dates it 2015, the year the reviews landed. The Financial Times review is the first major-press notice on her page.

Aftab later told Clash that the follow-up she first planned was meant to be edgier, groove-minded and more fun. She was not yet thinking about a record of grief.

years.h: Siren Islands on New Amsterdam Records
years.p: Released June 12, it is the ambient, electronic one. NPR put it on its list of the year's best electronic music, and the New York Times picked "Island No. 2" among 2018's best classical tracks.
years.xp: The same year, NPR ranked her song "Lullaby" at No. 150 on its list of the 200 greatest songs by 21st-century women. The New York Times and NPR were filing her in three different genre boxes at once, which is the whole problem and the whole point.

years.h: Aftab opens for Mitski at Brooklyn Steel
years.p: One of her biggest rooms to date is an indie-rock one, playing before Mitski in Brooklyn.

years.h: An Emmy for editing Armed With Faith
years.p: Aftab edited the documentary Armed With Faith, which won a News and Documentary Emmy for outstanding politics and government documentary.

eras.title: A record for Maher
eras.text: Aftab's younger brother Maher died in 2018. The record she was making changed shape, and it became her breakthrough. In between she recorded a trio album she would sit on for years.

years.src: The Skinny · NPR: How Arooj Aftab
years.h: Aftab, Vijay Iyer and Shahzad Ismaily record a trio album in a Brooklyn studio
years.p: The pianist Vijay Iyer and the bassist Shahzad Ismaily track improvised sessions that will not come out for four years.
years.xp: The Skinny reports the trio record was made in 2019 and held for release in early 2023. NPR says it was recorded at Ismaily's studio in Brooklyn and describes the group as music made collectively, in what they call "ritual time".

years.h: Latin Grammy for a backing vocal on Residente's single
years.p: Aftab sings on "Antes Que El Mundo Se Acabe" by the Puerto Rican rapper Residente, which won a Latin Grammy.

years.src: Wikipedia: Vulture Prince · Crack Magazine · Wikipedia: Arooj Aftab
years.h: Vulture Prince: seven songs, one brother
years.p: The album is dedicated to Maher Aftab and reset ghazals and poems around grief, with harp, violin, double bass and flugelhorn. Pitchfork gave it 8.2.
years.xp:
Aftab told Crack she set out to follow Bird Under Water with something edgier and groove-led, even leaning on afrobeat. After her brother's death, the record's central character turned somber, a passageway through which she could move her own grief.

Wikipedia credits contributions from the harpist Maeve Gilchrist, the guitarist Badi Assad and the percussionist Jamey Haddad. The Guardian ranked it No. 20 of 2021, with Laura Snapes calling Aftab the year's biggest musical revelation, and the Dutch paper de Volkskrant named it album of the year.

years.src: Wikipedia: Arooj Aftab · Stereogum: Arooj Aftab Interview
years.h: "Mohabbat" lands on Barack Obama's summer playlist
years.p: The eight-minute song from Vulture Prince shows up on the former president's list and on Time and New York Times best-of-2021 rankings.

years.h: Verve signs Aftab after Vulture Prince
years.p: Wikipedia puts the signing in late 2021: a New Amsterdam artist now on a Universal jazz label.

eras.title: The Grammy, and a trio out in the open
eras.text: A surprise win reset what a room expected from her. She played Coachella, sang at the Grammys, and finally released the trio record, which Pitchfork called Best New Music.

years.src: GRAMMY.com · Stereogum: Arooj Aftab Interview · Wikipedia: Arooj Aftab
years.h: "Mohabbat" wins Best Global Music Performance
years.p: At the 64th Grammys Aftab becomes the first Pakistani artist to win one. She was also nominated for Best New Artist.
years.xp:
Grammy.com reports she is the first Pakistani woman to win the award. Stereogum notes she was the first Pakistani woman nominated by the Recording Academy, in a general-field category.

Her own account of the record, from that Stereogum interview: she made a personal record she loved and did not think too much about it.

years.h: Coachella: the first Pakistani artist to play it
years.p: Crack credits her as the first Pakistani artist to perform at Coachella, and Wikipedia lists Glastonbury, Primavera Sound and Roskilde among her festival dates.

years.h: Pakistan gives her the Pride of Performance
years.p: President Arif Alvi awards her the country's top arts honor on the 75th independence day.

years.h: "Mehram" on Coke Studio with Asfar Hussain
years.p: She returns to Pakistan's biggest music franchise as a Grammy winner, singing "Mehram" with the musician Asfar Hussain.

years.h: First Pakistani artist to perform at the Grammys
years.p: She plays the ceremony, and is nominated again: Best Global Music Performance for "Udhero Na" with Anoushka Shankar.

years.src: Wikipedia: Love in Exile · NPR: How Arooj Aftab · Wikipedia: Arooj Aftab
years.h: Love in Exile with Vijay Iyer and Shahzad Ismaily
years.p: Released March 24 on Verve, a 75-minute trio record of voice, piano, electric bass and Moog. Pitchfork gave it 8.5 and Best New Music.
years.xp:
Wikipedia reports a Metacritic score of 85, five stars each from the Guardian and Mojo, and a No. 10 finish on the New York Times' year-end list, with Pitchfork placing it No. 25 of 2023. The trio has said they share responsibility for the music, which is what they credit for their freedom as individuals.

At the 66th Grammys the album was nominated for Best Alternative Jazz Album and "Shadow Forces" for Best Global Music Performance.

years.h: The trio plays "Eyes of the Endless" at NPR's Tiny Desk
years.p: Aftab sings, Iyer plays Fender Rhodes and piano, Ismaily plays bass and Moog, all in the moment, as NPR describes it.

eras.title: She makes a record about the night
eras.text: With two years on the road behind her, Aftab wrote and arranged a record for after dark, in a happier stretch than the last solo album. A video directed by an actor, a title she could not shake, and a guest list that included Elvis Costello.

years.h: "Raat Ki Rani": Tessa Thompson's first directing job
years.p: The first single and its video, released April 18, premiere with the album announcement.
years.xp: Wikipedia calls the video Tessa Thompson's directorial debut. The second single, "Whiskey", followed on May 7.

years.src: Wikipedia: Night Reign · Album of the Year: Night Reign · The FADER
years.h: Night Reign: Costello on Wurlitzer, Moor Mother on vocals
years.p: Released May 31 on Verve, 48 minutes of Pakistani folk and bebop in Urdu and English. Pitchfork's Andy Cush gave it 8.3 and called it a "wondrous fourth album".
years.xp:
Wikipedia credits Vijay Iyer on piano, Kaki King on guitar and Maeve Gilchrist on harp, with Elvis Costello on Wurlitzer and the poet Moor Mother on vocals. The FADER adds Gyan Riley on guitar, Darian Donovan Thomas on violin, Petros Klampanis on bass, Cautious Clay and Marc Anthony Thompson.

Per Album of the Year, Pitchfork's 83 sat in a critic average of 86; Metacritic aggregated 89. The FADER reports "Na Gul" and "Saaqi" are the first musical settings of the 18th-century Urdu poet Mah Laqa Bai Chanda, and that "Bolo Na" was written in high school and shelved as too cheesy.

years.big: The night became a great friend.
q: The night became a great friend.
years.src: The Quietus · The FADER · Crack Magazine
years.h: Two years, 200-plus shows, all of them after dark
years.p: Aftab told The Quietus that the shows, the jet lag and the flights all happen at night. The FADER counts more than 200 shows behind her when she wrote it.
years.xp: Crack noted earlier that she performs in darkness with silhouetted staging, so the title was less a pivot than a confession.

years.h: She curates Le Guess Who? in Utrecht, and books her father
years.p: Among her picks for the November 7–10 festival: Meshell Ndegeocello, Aja Monet, Dina El Wedidi, Noura Mint Seymali, Zsela and her own father.

years.src: Album of the Year: Pitchfork's 50 Best Albums of 2024
years.h: Pitchfork ranks Night Reign No. 17 of 2024
years.p: The album lands mid-table on Pitchfork's 50 Best Albums of 2024, seven places outside the top ten.

eras.title: More nominations, and a cover with Beck
eras.text: Aftab's fourth Grammy nominations cycle brought two more, and a humanitarian compilation brought a collaboration nobody predicted.

years.h: Two Grammy nominations for Night Reign
years.p: Best Alternative Jazz Album for the album, and Best Global Music Performance for "Raat Ki Rani", at the 67th ceremony.

years.h: Aftab and Beck cover "Lilac Wine" for War Child
years.p: The duet is on the Help(2) compilation, which raises money for War Child's work.
